vignette:
Since the hurricane that struck the Gulf Coast three years ago, Tane's life had narrowed in ways that made sense to him but left him feeling increasingly cut off. He was a 46-year-old auditor, a widower who had built his days around order, schedules, and careful review, and on the night of the storm that order vanished. He had been in a hotel for work, several floors up, when the power failed and the building went black. The wind screamed through broken seals, alarms cut in and out, and the stairwell filled with a damp, chemical smell from floodwater and generator fumes. He remembered gripping the rail in the dark, mouth full of a metallic, dirty taste, waiting for updates that never came, convinced each delay meant the building was giving way and there was nothing he could do to stop it.

In the months afterward, the parts of ordinary life that should have felt good or neutral began to unsettle him most. If he caught himself relaxing at home after dinner, or felt unexpectedly happy during a quiet evening, he would tense almost immediately, as if calm were the moment danger slipped in unnoticed. Those moments did not just unsettle him; they seemed to prove something to him about the world, that safety was a trick and that he was still the kind of man who could be blindsided without warning. Nighttime was especially difficult. Waking in darkness brought back the sense of being trapped in that powerless hotel, and certain physical locations-parking garages, stairwells, older office buildings, unfamiliar client sites-could make his body react before he had time to think. When that happened he would light a cigarette, step outside, keep moving, and avoid settling long enough to feel anything; he had also stopped talking with other people about the hurricane or what followed, because even brief conversation about it seemed to pull him too close to something he could not control.

The triggers also sharpened his sense that threat was always close. Silence in a building, especially after business hours, no longer felt peaceful to Tane; unusual quiet made him brace, listening for what was about to go wrong. If an elevator stalled for a moment, if a report upload took too long, if a colleague was late answering a message, his mind leapt to catastrophe. At client visits he often stayed near exits and resisted going into parts of a building he did not know well, telling himself he needed to assess the danger first. The same moments could bring back the disaster with disturbing sensory force. In the dark, or when he entered certain locations, he could suddenly smell the rank mix of floodwater and fuel again and taste the foul metallicness that had filled his mouth that night; at times the memory was so extreme it felt unreal, as if he were describing something that had happened to someone else. Afterward, those sensations seemed to spread the storm into more of his life, so that darkness, stale air, and unfamiliar buildings no longer felt like neutral details but like cues he had to treat as dangerous.

What had settled most deeply was his conviction that the world was dangerous and that he was fundamentally helpless inside it. He had come to believe that bad things happened without warning and that no amount of preparation could truly stop them. Once he saw life that way, ordinary situations he would once have dismissed-a quiet corridor, a delayed response, a dim hallway-began to snag on his attention and take on the charge of warning signs. That belief made him scan harder in silence and grow more alarmed by delays, because any pause seemed like proof that disaster was already unfolding somewhere out of sight. It also colored the way he remembered the hurricane: the sensory fragments arrived with more force when he was caught in that helpless frame of mind, and the very extremity of the memory reinforced his feeling that normal rules did not apply and safety could not be trusted. On days when he was most braced for something to go wrong, the memory came faster and harder, as if the sense of danger itself were pulling the hotel night back into the room with him.

Over time his ways of coping deepened the problem. He smoked more heavily during the workday, especially before entering unfamiliar office buildings, and structured his schedule to avoid lingering anywhere that might let him relax. Because he kept leaving, bracing, and dosing himself with cigarettes instead of finding out a place was tolerable, his body never seemed to learn anything new; the danger continued to feel immediate, as if all that vigilance were still necessary. As an auditor, he used to be known for his ease on site, but now he rushed inspections, asked to switch assignments, and avoided small talk with clients if it drifted toward weather, emergencies, or personal life. Refusing to talk and never letting himself settle brought a temporary sense of control, yet afterward he felt more dead inside, more convinced something essential in him had shut down. That numbness seemed to confirm his bleak view of himself and the world, and it left him even less willing to risk ease, pleasure, or openness with other people.

The pattern had tightened further in the past year. Because he spent so much effort staying guarded, even moments of happiness had started to feel like triggers in their own right, almost a warning sign that he was about to be blindsided. The more he avoided relaxing and kept to known places, the more foreign and dangerous unfamiliar settings became. His efforts to stay safe had gradually marked whole categories of places and states of mind as risky, until even the route around a stairwell or the decision not to linger in a quiet building made those things feel loaded before he had even entered them. The more he scanned for danger, the more easily sensory fragments of the hurricane broke through; and once those smells and tastes returned, he became certain he was right not to trust silence, darkness, or delay.

Tane sought help only after he nearly walked out of an overnight audit at a downtown hotel when a brief power fluctuation dimmed the hallway lights. Standing there with a cigarette in his shaking hand, tasting that old metallic bitterness, he was struck by how small his life had become. What frightened him most was not just another memory, but the sense that he would remain trapped in vigilance and emptiness, unable to feel safe even in the rare moments that should have brought relief. What he hopes for, though he says it cautiously, is to stop living as if the storm is still deciding what to take from him.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not clearly state in one paragraph that triggers themselves lead to or intensify Tane’s negative appraisals or beliefs.
The vignette does not clearly state in one paragraph that Tane’s negative appraisals cause ordinary situations or cues to become triggers.
The vignette does not clearly state in one paragraph that the traumatic memory itself makes cues or situations become triggers.
The vignette does not clearly state in one paragraph that Tane’s sense of threat directly brings on the trauma memory.
The vignette does not clearly state in one paragraph that Tane’s avoidance or other maladaptive strategies increase or create triggers.
The vignette does not clearly state in one paragraph that Tane’s maladaptive coping directly heightens his sense of threat.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not clearly state in one paragraph that triggers themselves lead to or intensify Tane’s negative appraisals or beliefs.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not clearly state in one paragraph that Tane’s negative appraisals cause ordinary situations or cues to become triggers.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not clearly state in one paragraph that the traumatic memory itself makes cues or situations become triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette does not clearly state in one paragraph that Tane’s sense of threat directly brings on the trauma memory.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette does not clearly state in one paragraph that Tane’s avoidance or other maladaptive strategies increase or create triggers.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The vignette does not clearly state in one paragraph that Tane’s maladaptive coping directly heightens his sense of threat.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."
